parsed.stack: iOS-only for v1 specifically to sit on Apple's free on-device and Private Cloud Compute tier under the Small Business Program (Swift/SwiftUI, Apple Foundation Models + VisionKit OCR for nameplates); cloud frontier vision only as a fallback for unreadable shots; the one real recurring cost is a parts-compatibility lookup, which needs a web search or a parts data feed per model number; CloudKit for the user's own record so there is almost no server; Stripe via StoreKit; App Store.
milestones: Week 1-2: capture and record - photograph the shutoff, heater label and panel, on-device OCR of the nameplate, and a dated per-unit record that works offline.
Week 3-4: identification - make/model resolution from the plate plus a confidence score, with a manual correct-it path that feeds back into the record.
Week 5-6: 'what fits it' - anode rod, TP valve, thermocouple, breaker type for the identified model, with sourced links and an explicit 'not sure' state instead of a guess.
Week 7: shareable record - a clean PDF/link a landlord can hand to a plumber or a tenant, which is the professional-recommendation loop.
Week 8-9: free tier at one unit / 10 photos, paid at $7 for unlimited units and the shareable record, App Store review.
parsed.riskiest_technical_assumption: That the on-device vision model reads a corroded, badly lit water-heater nameplate into a correct make and model number at the 80-in-100 rate this needs, since every cloud fallback both costs money and breaks the offline-in-a-basement promise.
parsed.cheapest_way_to_test_that_assumption: Shoot 100 phone photos of nameplates, shutoffs and panels across five real rental units in the light that is actually there, run them through the on-device model in a TestFlight-less scratch app over a weekend, and score against the plates read by hand.
